utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Mr. Tieger and Mr. Robinson, given the prior notice, the Chamber has decided not to sit on Friday, 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I echo that, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, everyone. Good morning, your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bjelica. Can you tell us whether there was some military organising in your municipality before the war and if so who was engaged in that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war in Sokolac municipality there was the TO as well as the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Ministry of Defence had the task of providing manpower to -- for the 216th Motorised Brigade which was part of the JNA. There were no other formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How about the SDA? Did the Muslim side have anything in 1991, and what did you know about it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the Muslim side, we had information that the Muslim people were arming themselves in the territory of Sokolac municipality. We had such information as early as June 1991, when we learned that Muslims were being organised through a military wing of the SDA which was called the Patriotic League. In addition to the Patriotic League, there were also the Green Berets. We also had intelligence that the political leadership of the SDA had made a decision to establish a military structure, a military formation, which was supposed to protect the Muslim people and which was also to be used to defend the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina when such time came about. It functioned under the auspices of Mr. Izetbegovic, and its operational part was led by Ejup Ganic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the second name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the military activity was led by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, could you repeat from where you mentioned Mr. Izetbegovic and Ejup Ganic. The interpreters were not able to hear the names of other persons. And speak very slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. It functioned the under the auspices of the leadership of the SDA. It was directly led by Alija Izetbegovic. The political part, political supervision of this newly formed formation was in the hands of Ejup Ganic and Mr. Mehmed [as interpreted]. The military part was in the hands of Sefer Halilovic, who before that had been a senior officer of the JNA in the territory of our municipality of Sokolac. There was a unit of the Patriotic League which was organised by a member of the security service of the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the time, it was the staff of the Patriotic League which after the outbreak of conflicts transformed itself into the army of BiH. His name was Mevludin Smajic. He provided a statement on the 24th of September, 1992, to the "Oslobodjenje" newspaper. I think that article was entitled "The Voice of a Patriot" or "Mevludin Smajic, the Story of a Patriot." The date is the 24th of September, 1992, it means it is already the fall of 1992 when the war was well under way in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He stated that for the entire last year, that is to say 1991, the entire previous year, he worked on arming the Muslim people in the territory of Sokolac municipality. He also stated that he basically went to Vitez every other day, bringing in explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you -- well, we have the newspaper. We'll see it in a moment, but did you learn it from him, or when was it that you heard of it for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The public security station had intelligence because we had acted upon some reports of neighbours when we were informed that there were weapons in the house of Emir Klica. At the time he provided a statement to the police at the station in Sokolac. He stated that he was a commander of a Patriotic League company. They found a radio device on him as well as a PM, as well as some other weapons. He said that they had some 866 people on the list out of whom 40 per cent were well armed. He also stated that they had sent their young men to be trained in Libya, in Kumrovec, and Remetinac and another two places in Croatia where there were camps for the training of terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mehmed, the name is actually Omer Behmen, which is on page 2 in the transcript, Omer Behmen when we asked Mr. Bjelica to repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have in e-court 1D14014.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was Mevludin Smajic's occupation? What was his position?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked at the Ministry of Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina. For a while, I think he was in charge of security detail, providing security for Mr. Cengic, Delimustafic, and other prominent personnel. He worked in the state security of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was he an authorised official? Did he have an ID?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we zoom in on the part in the box so that you can tell us whether that is the statement he provided to the newspaper, and how did it fit into the information the police had at the time when the weapons were discovered in 1991? No. No. Towards the bottom of the page in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please put the frame in the centre of the picture.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is it. A member of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mevludin Smajic. He used to work -- or he worked on the arming of members of the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is the article in question. They also published a book about the establishment of the Patriotic League where they described things in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber whose newspaper is the "Oslobodjenje"?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was published in Sarajevo, in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war. One could not get it in the territory of RS.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3224, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions of Mr. Bjelica at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At paragraph 8 of your statement, you discuss the SAO Romanija. You said that you were a member of the SAO Romanija Assembly, and you stated that only one Assembly session was held at which Assembly bodies and executive organs were elected, that they did not function later on so that the existence of the SAO Romanija was declarative in character. Now, you said there was only one SAO Romanija Assembly session. When was that session?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the precise date. It is true that there was only one Assembly session of the SAO Romanija. The Assembly was established, and the prime minister of the SAO government was elected. It never met after that, however, because the seat of the SAO Romanija was in Sarajevo, and members of the Assembly came from different municipalities, not only from Sokolac. So as the situation developed and tensions rose, there were no conditions in place to hold such Assembly session. So on that session the SAO Romanija was proclaimed, but it never -- it was never followed up by any other session.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 01473, please. Mr. Bjelica, these are minutes of a session of the Assembly of the SAO Romanija held in Pale on the 11th of December, 1991, and the first agenda item is adoption of the decision on appointment of members of the SAO Romanija government. Is this the session that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that a decision was made at that session to appoint Mr. Blagojevic to be the prime minister as is stated here. So this is most likely the session in question, although I'm not positive.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we go down to the -- towards the bottom of the page, it says -- there's a statement by the representative from Sokolac, and it says: "At the last meeting we agreed that all candidates for ministers should attend this session." Now, that reference to at the last meeting indicates that there was a previous session of the Assembly of the SAO Romanija; right? So this would have been at least the second session?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not an Assembly session, the other meeting. It says -- it is correct the Assembly of the SAO Romanija, but it is the minutes of a meeting rather than of an Assembly session. It was probably a smaller body which met representing the 22 municipalities. So it was not an Assembly session. There was only one Assembly session, that is certain, but there may have been other meetings held by the various government candidates, but there was only one SAO Romanija Assembly session. Perhaps this was a consultative meeting and that is what is referred to as the previous one. Usually people are agreed upon, those who will be in charge of activities in the municipalities, and they have to agree on the assigning of position and which municipality will have what position.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. My time is very limited, which is why I interrupted you. If you could try to keep your answers focused and concisely directed to the question. The -- now, you said that the SAO Romanija was declarative in character. However, the SAO Romanija government, which was established at this session, held government sessions and carried out government activities, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government only issued certain communiques if they met and there was a crisis and as needed. For example, Mr. Zugic, the minister of information would issue such communiques or the Prime Minister Drago Blagojevic. They may have issued a few communiques for the public, and it always came from either the Ministry of Information or the prime minister himself. There were no other activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 24874, please, and I would tender the minutes of the Assembly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6250, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, if we could go -- sorry. Mr. Bjelica, you can see this is the government of the SAO Romanija work programme for 1992, and if we could go to the next page in the B/C/S. It refers to the agreement reached at the second session of the government of the SAO Romanija held in Pale on the 15th of January, 1992. So that indicates that by the 15th of January, the government of the SAO Romanija had held at least two sessions?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could slide the text over so that Mr. Bjelica can see this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can you read it now, Mr. Bjelica? And it says that all the ministers of the government were obliged to produce 1992 working plans, and then it gives details about what those plans were to cover.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could scroll through the document, you can see that there are detailed plans for government -- SAO Romanija government activities in the areas of economy, agriculture, forestry, industry and energy.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could scroll through the document so Mr. Bjelica can at least see the headings.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Traffic, spatial planning, finances, trade, tourism and catering, health, information system, justice, science, education, culture, and sport. This document makes clear, Mr. Bjelica, that this was not just a government that issued communiques. They were involved in governmental activities; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I see this for the first time. As regards the SAO Romanija, there was the association of municipalities of Han Pijesak, Sokolac, Pale, and Rogatica which was then expanded, but it never came to life. It had existed back in the times of Communism and the SFRY. There were such districts encompassing associations of municipalities. Now, this programme never saw the light of day, and I see it now for the first time. This is completely new to me. But also there's nothing special about it. It's a programme. Maybe drafted by the prime minister. I don't know. I've never seen it, and I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, let's look at something you have seen before. It's 65 ter 05360, the minutes of the Sokolac Crisis Staff session held on the 7th of May, 1992, and a document that is referenced in your statement at paragraph 35. You can see that the third item on the agenda for this meeting is the status of ethnic Muslim workers. And if we go to page 2 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S. And this is the second paragraph from the bottom in the English and the second paragraph from the top in the B/C/S. There's an intervention by you. It says: "Milovan Bjelica participated in the discussion and stressed that it is necessary to deal with any kind of provocations immediately. He proposed that the Muslim citizens who are military conscripts be called up as well as to introduce a compulsory work service for them." And then at page 3 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S, so the next page -- sorry, it's page 4 of the English as well. Directly the last paragraph above item 4. It says: "Concerning the suggestion of Milovan Bjelica that the ethnic Muslim citizens be mobilised, it was concluded that the proposal needs more consideration and that this question together with the question about the loyalty of the Muslim citizens should be resolved uniformly at the level of the SAO Romanija." Now, Mr. Bjelica, you were at this meeting. This is a reflection of the fact that the SAO Romanija was a decision-making body; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not correct. This is for the territory of the SAO Romanija, including Ilijas, Olovo, Han Pijesak, et cetera. So it's the same territory. I did propose that members of Muslim ethnicity be called up who refused to respond to mobilisation to be assigned to work in the companies of Romanija and Sumarstvo, the forestry company. This simply encompasses the territory of the SAO Romanija, but it is not its document or the body itself, the organisation itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, this document refers explicitly to the SAO Romanija and says that a decision should be made at that level. Who else is going to make a decision at the level of the SAO Romanija other than a body of the SAO Romanija?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Can it be read out precisely what needs to be done, because there is no word "decision" in the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I read out the text. It's in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may. As regards the proposal of Milovan Bjelica, this is not my conclusion, but I did suggest that Muslim conscripts be called up for work obligation. Based on this proposal after thorough discussion at the meeting, it was concluded that my proposal deserved a second thought and that at the level of the SAO Romanija a uniform decision -- conclusion needs to be made in order to take up position in terms of loyalty of Muslim citizens. This is not a conclusion. There was war in the territory and the SAO Romanija could not function because its seat was in Sarajevo in the federation. At that time, it was controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Patriotic League, the Green Berets, and the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and others. So it's got nothing to do with anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, the government document we just referred to stated that it was issued in Pale. So presumably just like the republic level government, the SAO Romanija level government moved from Sarajevo to Pale; no?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president or the prime minister of the SAO Romanija government lived in Sarajevo. That's perhaps why he invited several colleagues and held a meeting. The seat was in Sarajevo. The Pale seat was never made official. As for the other institutions, for security reasons they had to be moved to Pale. For the government of the SAO Romanija, it was not necessary for it to function. It could not function because the territory could not be reached like in Ilijas, Olovo, Stari Grad, Novi Grad, Trnovo, all those municipalities that were members of the SAO Romanija. So that's why the SAO Romanija could not function.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript don't reflect that the territory was intersected. But your Excellencies, I'm looking at the translation, and I can say that the translation does not reflect the original. The translation is a bit creative. It's more of a summary than the word-for-word translation of the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could now go to 65 ter 19834, and I would tender the government document we saw previously, which was 65 ter 05355.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the 65 ter number of the previous document?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The one we just looked at is a Defence associated exhibit so I don't tender that, but the one before that was 05355 -- oh, sorry, 24874. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we object to the admission of this document because the witness didn't say anything about it and hadn't seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's an impeachment document, Your Honour. The witness stated that the SAO Romanija was -- organs were declarative in character and the document indicate contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't know anything about the provenance of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow your statement, Mr. Robinson, about the provenance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you challenging the authenticity of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We don't know anything about the authenticity. Perhaps the Prosecution can provide us with some information about it, but since the witness had nothing to say about the document, we don't have any information about its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we upload that document again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've not seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Although you didn't see this document before, do you agree that this is a document produced by the SAO Romanija government programme for 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was not at the Assembly. The SAO Romanija Assembly met only once. I cannot accept this document. I don't know anything about it. I've not seen this document before, so I can't agree with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At the moment we'll mark it for identification until we hear more about the provenance of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P6251, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you are not tendering 5360? That's admitted already, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3227, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, I'll just change course slightly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 05355.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bjelica, this is a document issued by the SAO Romanija Ministry of Defence, dated the 10th of February, 1992, about obtaining medical and sanitary equipment for the need of the wartime hospital. You can see that it is signed and stamped by the vice-president of the government, Milan Tupajic, the minister of defence, Dragomir Krstovic, and the commander of the SAO Romanija Territorial Defence Slobodan Batinic, and the document indicates that the SAO Romanija ministry of defence had created a list of medical equipment needs for wartime hospitals, was requesting assistance from the addressees in procuring this assistance, and had assigned coordinators to procure the requested equipment. Again, this is evidence that the SAO Romanija government was a functioning governmental body, not just a body as you stated that issued communiques; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I've not seen this document before. I can't comment upon it. I've not seen it before. There's nothing out of the ordinary in it, but I've not seen it before. I was not a government member. As far as I know, and as I've already told you, a communique here and there was issued on behalf of the government, and as for the Assembly, I've already told you what I know. I've not seen this document before ever.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6252, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go now to 65 ter 19834. And this on the B/C/S is towards the bottom right-hand side of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, this is an announcement by the SAO Romanija Crisis Staff, stating that the Serbian people in this area have definitely lost their confidence in the possibility of a political agreement with the Muslim people. Now, it is correct, is it not, that by the 5th of March, 1992, when this announcement was issued that the SAO Romanija leadership had lost confidence in any political agreement with the Muslims, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can the document please be zoomed in a little. I'm talking about the article.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, my question is, Mr. Bjelica, do you agree that by the 5th of March, 1992, the SAO Romanija leadership had lost confidence in any political agreement with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this was issued by the Crisis Staff of the SAO Romanija. That did not exist. I don't know who issued this. As far as I'm personally concerned, this article speaks about a body that did not exist at all, this SAO Romanija Crisis Staff did not exist, but after the member of Nikola Gardovic who was a wedding party member, the Serbs started believing that they would see the same fate as in 1990 -- 40 and 1995 -- 1 and that they would all be killed. I agree with that. And as for this article, I don't know who may have sent it to the media, but I agree that the whole situation was reminiscent of the slaughters that happened in 1914 and then in 1941, and that was an additional reason for the Serbs to become more homogeneous, to try and defend themselves, because after the killing of Nikola Gardovic who was a wedding party guest, the authorities in Sarajevo did not react. They, rather, let the murderer escape. On the 4th and on the 5th of March, I believe that the president, President Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm interrupting you because your answer is straying far away from my question, which was very simple. Let me put it this way: You were shown this document in the Krajisnik case and you were asked whether the SAO Romanija leadership had lost confidence in the possibility of any political agreement with the Muslims, and you answered yes. That's what you say in the Krajisnik case, and that's true; right? That's at 65 ter 2487 --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] I said that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure the witness has answered correctly because of the overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, that's what you answered in the Krajisnik case, and that's correct; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, this is what I said: When it comes to the SAO Romanija Crisis Staff, I'm not familiar with that body, but I agree with the text that I can see before me. After the murder of Nikola Gardovic, the Serbian --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bjelica, stop.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the wedding party member, the Serbs started fearing --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Stop, Mr. Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, I'm asking the questions here.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please do not -- do not raise your voice. I'm a witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a witness here and I want to be protected. I want to be protected here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, you are fully protected. Don't worry about it. Shall we upload the Krajisnik transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's 65 ter 24876, page 123.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And at the top of the page you were asked: "That is the case in SAO Romanija, isn't it, Mr. Bjelica, that by the 5th of March, 1992, the leadership of SAO Romanija had lost confidence in the possibility of any political agreement with Muslims?" And then you start discussing the article. You say: "I don't know who declared this or who [sic] signed this --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that the witness does not read English, read it in full, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I was just going to move to where he said yes, and the question was: "Now take your eyes away from the article and listen to the question and answer the question. They had lost confidence in the possibility of a political agreement with the Muslims, hadn't they? "A. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's fair to read out the previous passage.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He said: "I don't remember this. I don't know who declared this or signed this, whether this was Mr. Blagojevic or Djukic. I don't know. But at any rate, this was not discussed at any forum. This was an announcement of a personal kind." That's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, if you feel that he should see that, that's fine. And then the question was: "Q. I'm sorry, Mr. Bjelica. You have to listen to my questions and my question was specific. It was that the people, the Serb people of SAO Romanija had lost confidence in the possibility of a political agreement. "Now take your eyes away from the article and listen to the question and answer the question: They had lost confidence in the possibility of a political agreement with the Muslims hadn't they? "A. Yes." That's what you said this Krajisnik; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm repeating it today. I said it at the Krajisnik case. I don't know who signed the document. I said that at the Krajisnik case, and I am saying this today in the President Karadzic case. My statement is still the same. You did not allow me to finish. After the murder of Nikola Gardovic on the 5th of March, that's the day you mentioned, and you asked me whether we lost confidence on the 4th and on the 5th of March. The apartments of well-known Serbs would be marked, and that would be the dark night for the Serbs. Then General Kukanjac and Alija Izetbegovic invited people to calm down, for tensions to be lowered, because there was a state of general chaos among the Serbian people in Sarajevo, and of course needless to say that the confidence was lost because if a person was killed at a wedding and nobody reacted, what could one expect? It happened before the eyes of thousands of spectators. Still that person was not arrested. That person, the murderer, he was allowed to walk free.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If you could try to keep your answers concise and directly focus on the question, please. I'd like 65 ter -- or sorry, P5802, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution offering that article?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, this is a transcript of a conversation between you and Mr. Karadzic on the 13th of December, 1991, and before you read it, you said at paragraph 24 of your statement that the Bosnian Serbs supported the JNA and that several companies from Sokolac went to the Croatian front at the orders of the command. In fact, you and Dr. Karadzic in 1991 were directly involved in sending forces to the Croatian front, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. Mr. Karadzic did not participate in that at all. Why would the party president be involved in sending troops to the front line in Croatia in 1991? It's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could ask you to just read this conversation before I ask you the next question. It's quite short. You can just read it to yourself. It's three pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Five pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, three in the English, five in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we can just scroll through so that you can read it.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this document, this document is an intercept of a conversation between myself and Mr. Karadzic, and then the president of the municipality got involved in the conversation. This is about mobilisation, the mobilisation of the 216 Motorised Mountain Brigade. It is correct that President Karadzic advocated the policy of preserving Yugoslavia and of supporting the Yugoslav People's Army, because the Yugoslav People's Army was the guarantor of peace and the survival of the people in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. The 216th Motorised Brigade had its zone of responsibility in Romanija. It was mostly replenished from -- by people from Sokolac, Han Pijesak, and Vlasenica. In Vlasenica there was a large number of Muslims who --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you because I didn't ask you about the zone of responsibility of the 216th Brigade. When Dr. Karadzic says to you: "Do you have any spare troops? Could you send one company to Uzelac?," and you respond: "Right now, Doctor, I can't until I've checked. We have two more units in Minici [phoen] and Vukovar," it's clear that whether or not this is talking about the JNA or not, you and Dr. Karadzic, two SDS officials, are involved in sending forces to fight in Croatia, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA, the 216th Motorised Mountain Brigade under the command of General Milosevic and -- no, no. That's not correct. You are misinterpreting things. We encouraged them. I personally invited military conscripts to report to the legal unit of the JNA to defend the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia in Croatia. The JNA was still active in the territory of Yugoslavia. I don't know about Slovenia. In any case, they were there to defend the state that we took our oath to. I asked them to join the legal army and to replace those who deserted and who were Muslims and who deserted from the ranks. I wanted to replenish the formation, the battalion who had to Vukovar on the orders of the Supreme Command of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, i.e., the General Staff in Belgrade. They had a chain of command, and when a superior command sent people to a certain locality, they had to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your position is clear. At paragraph 28 of your statement, you said the Sokolac Crisis Staff was formed according to the instructions of the RS government to form Crisis Staffs, and you refer to Exhibit D2676, those government instructions. Now, under the terms of your own sworn statement, that proposition is impossible because the government instructions you refer to are dated the 26th of April, 1992, and you discuss in your statement numerous Crisis Staff documents dated well before this time, for example, D3176, a Crisis Staff order from the 10th of April. Now, you agree with me that it's impossible that the Sokolac Crisis Staff which was clearly functioning as of the 10th of April could have been formed pursuant to government instructions dated the 26th of April?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have my reservations. I can't remember the date. That's what I always repeat. I can't remember that it was set up on the 26th of April. The Crisis Staff acted in lieu of local authorities up until the summer of 1992, and then the executive power duties were assumed by the executive council. In any -- in any case, members of the Crisis Staff elected -- were elected by virtue --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down. It's impossible to interpret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, you're speaking too fast for the interpreters to follow. Could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor is speeding. When it comes to the Crisis Staff, the Crisis Staff in Sokolac was set up in the spring of 1992, and it consisted of the president of the Municipal Assembly, the president of the Executive Board, the chief of the public security station -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about the composition of the Crisis Staff. It was a very simple question. Do you agree with me that it is impossible that the Sokolac Crisis Staff, which was clearly functioning as of the 10th of April, 1992, was established pursuant to government instructions dated the 26th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the spring of that year, the spring of 1992. I don't know if what -- if it was on the 26th of April, the 1st of April, the 1st of May, the 25th of May, I'm not sure. And I already told you that I am not sure about the date. I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your own statement references numerous Crisis Staff documents dated well before the 26th of April. Do you now deny the authenticity of those documents that you commented on and were tendered through you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not denying. I'm not denying any document that I commented upon, but you would have to jog my memory about the date. That's the only thing in dispute. I may be wrong about the dates, but I'm not denying knowledge about any of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I am jogging your memory, Mr. Bjelica. I'm telling you that the documents in your statement indicate that the Sokolac Crisis Staff was functioning as of the 10th of April, 1992. Now, do you agree that it's impossible that that Crisis Staff was established pursuant to government instructions dated the 26th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Please clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In light of the time, Mr. Bjelica, I'm going to move on. Now, at paragraph 18 of your statement you said that as far as you know, the Variant A and B document was never delivered to the authorities in the entire Romanija region. The Chamber has received evidence indicating that at the end of December 1991, a Serb Municipal Assembly was created in Rogatica pursuant to the Variant A and B instructions, and that's P3407. In other words, Variant A and B was received and implemented in Rogatica according to the documents. Now, did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked about Sokolac. I did not talk about Rogatica and I don't know what happened in Rogatica. I know that this document was not in Sokolac, and that's what I said at President Krajisnik's trial too, and I also sent an official letter to you from the directorate of the Serb Democratic Party stating that this document was never before any one of the organs of the party. It was never discussed at any one of the organs of the party. Now, for a number of pensioned officers to write this document and to send that to their compatriots in certain areas, well, the document as far as I found out later, it was actually copied from a document that was created by Croatian and Muslim officers for their municipalities where they were in the position that the Serbs were in where this document was found, but this is not a document of the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, that's --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, please. In line 13, it was not recorded correctly. The witness said "I sent you an official document from the Serb Democratic Party." It wasn't to the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I sent it to the Office of the Prosecutor when I was director of the Serb Democratic Party, and it's been over ten years.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Let's look at that letter. That's 65 ter 24873. On page 1 there's a letter from the ICTY Prosecution asking for a distribution list for the 19 December 1991 Main Board instructions, otherwise known as Variant A and B. And then your letter is attached.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask whether Variant A and B is mentioned at all in Prosecutor Blewitt's letter? I haven't found it anywhere.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot follow what the witness is saying because he spoke at the same time Mr. Karadzic spoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, when Mr. Karadzic's words are being translated, please refrain from making any statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's common ground that the 19 December 1991 SDS Main Board instructions for the organisation and activity organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina is the Variant A and B document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me, Mr. President. With respect to this particular document, we are going to object to its use at this trial because it was not disclosed to us until yesterday, and we had made a motion pursuant to Rule 66(B) which you had granted ordering the Prosecution to have disclosed all documents authored by witnesses, enumerated witnesses, including this one, and there was a dead-line for that that was I think about a year ago and this document was not disclosed, and so given that we didn't see it until yesterday we would ask that it not be used and not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Can I hear from you, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I'm somewhat surprised. This objection is true. This document was disclosed yesterday. This document was a public exhibit in the Krajisnik case, and it was in fact shown to this witness in the Krajisnik case and discussed in his testimony. I would assume that the Defence would have read this witness's prior testimony in the Krajisnik case. If they were interested in this document, it was readily available to them. When I -- that -- and in fact that is exactly how it came to my attention, from my reading of the Krajisnik testimony. Then when I saw the document, I realised it had no ERN number and that led me to think it may not have been picked up in our earlier searches and I asked that it be disclosed immediately, which it was, and the Defence had at least some time to incorporate this document into their preparations. And, again, in any event this is entirely -- the position that the witness has stated in this document is exactly the position he stated in his prior testimony which the Defence has, so there's no prejudice here and this objection has no real merit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we can see how easy it is for people to miss --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We can see how easily it is for people to miss things since the Prosecution missed this during its disclosure searches for this witness and we also missed it, so we don't -- we apologise for the fact that we didn't pick it up. But nevertheless, it was required to have been disclosed to us a long time ago, so I would ask that you first make a finding that the Prosecution has violated Rule -- it's disclosure obligations under Rule 66(B) by failing to provide this document within the prescribed time. With respect to prejudice, again, it's something that we should have seen, but we have over 2 million pages of disclosure already, and we -- it's easy for us to miss things, and we don't think that the issue of prejudice ought to be determinative. If the Prosecution had disclosed this earlier to us we wouldn't have missed, so it's our position that it should be excluded and there should be an explicit finding of disclosure violation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to read it, but the Chamber will rise for 15 minutes and resume at 25 past. We will have another 15 minutes' break before the lunch break.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I just wanted to inform the Court: As I mentioned earlier, I ensured that this document when I came across it was disclosed out of an abundance of caution because it had no ERN number, so I wasn't sure it had been disclosed previously. While the Court was recessing we've checked our records and the document was disclosed on the 25th of January, 2013, it had an ERN number and was disclosed then to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. So obviously we don't know what we have and what we don't have and I apologise for that. We accept the fact that it was disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But further, Mr. Robinson, you referred to Rule 66(B) disclosure. Yes, I'm looking at this, because we do not have access to the e-court while we are logged on in the courtroom. Yes, indeed, you referred to Rule 66(B) disclosure, but in your previous motion this witness was never listed as Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, this witness was included in a letter of the 10th of August, 2012, specifically as number six of witnesses whom the Prosecution had undertaken to provide in addition to those that were listed in the Chamber's order. So he was covered by the Rule 66(B )request but not specifically mentioned in your order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. In any event, it resolves everything. Shall we continue. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, if we could go -- well, you can see it if we go to the next page in the English just to look at the last two sentences of this letter that you wrote in November 2001 where it says that the Main Board, as well as any other SDS body, never considered or instructed the organisation and activation of Serb people in BiH at its sessions. We were informed that such instructions with given by a certain number of retired officials -- officers, sorry, of the former Yugoslav People's Army. Now, is that still your position regarding the Variant A and B document today?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I signed this document too.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The Chamber has received a great deal of evidence to the contrary, and I would refer to P2589, the references at paragraphs 20 to 30 of that report, and that evidence includes SDS members speaking openly about the Variant A and B instructions at Assembly sessions. Now, at this point you had been -- when you wrote this letter in 2001 you were the director of the SDS as you said, and you have been an SDS member more or less since its inception. Now, you must have known, Mr. Bjelica, that what you were saying here is false and you were just putting forward what was then the party line about this document; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct, what you said just now, because not in any archives, nowhere in the archives of the Serb Democratic Party was this document found as received, registered, or that it was discussed by the party organs. So it is not reflected in any one of the records. Now, whether somebody distributed it personally, privately, that I don't know, but it's not in the organs of the party and that is clearly stated in this letter, in this reply that was sent. Nowhere. I stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, when you said it was never discussed by the party organs, I guess you're not aware of the speech of the Jajce municipal president at the 33rd Assembly session where he said: "If we go back a little and recall the material which came from the Main Board for work in the field, there was Variant A, Variant B." And then he says: "When according to instructions we were to form the Serbian municipality of Jajce on the orders of Dr. Karadzic and yourself," and he's speaking to Mr. Krajisnik, "I conducted talks with all the Assembly men in the joint Assembly who were Serbs," and then he refers to speaking to Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik in Sarajevo about what he was to do to implement the instructions. That's P1377, page 148. You're not aware of that discussion at a party organ about the Variant A and B document, are you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that, because nowhere is there any record of this kind of discussion at an Assembly meeting. I'm talking about what is official. It is not contained in any document. And now somebody taking part in a discussion, not all discussions are reflected in the record. Perhaps this was an informal conversation, but I claim to you with full responsibility that in the archives of the Serb Democratic Party this document does not exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In we could go to 65 ter 05382, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I could intervene, Ms. Gustafson. Do you see the last paragraph here, Mr. Bjelica? The last sentence. You said, I quote: "We were informed that such instructions were given by a certain number of retired officers of the former Yugoslav People's Army." I find it very unclear. Could you expand what you meant by this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a responsible individual and as director of the directorate of the Serb Democratic Party, the ruling party in that period of time when this document was requested, respecting this institution of the court and of the Office of the Prosecutor, I asked a number of friends from the party whether they knew anything about this document because it wasn't contained in the archives. I asked the then minister of defence, Mr. Subotic, Bogdan Subotic, General Subotic, I asked him whether he knew anything about this document. General Subotic, Bogdan, said to me that this document was never adopted, never considered, but he knew that a number of retired officers of the former JNA wrote this document on their own and that they allegedly sent it to a number of people in certain municipalities that they had originally hailed from and that in such way as persons with experience, military experience, they sent this document to the places where they had come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So first question for you, Mr. Bjelica, is that when you said "we were informed," the informant was Mr. Subotic? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Because I investigated the matter in order to give the most complete answer possible to this institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And what did you mean by a certain number of retired officers? How many of them, and then who are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, I don't know. That's what General Subotic said to me, Bogdan. I did not investigate it further. I was asked whether there was any such thing in the archives of the Serb Democratic Party, whether such a document had been registered, and I claim with full responsibility that it hadn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As a responsible person, as you said, I would have expected you to ask Mr. Subotic who were they, who they were. Why did you not ask Mr. Subotic further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the question that was put to me was whether this was contained in the archives of the Serb Democratic Party and whether there were minutes from the session of the Assembly where this matter had been considered. No. But in order to help in terms of this answer where this document came from, then I did ask a number of people from the party. Most of them were not aware of this document. And then I asked the most adequate person as far as this issue was concerned in my view, General Bogdan Subotic, who was minister of defence during the war, and this is the answer that he gave to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And still now at this moment, you do not know who they were and how it was circulated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Back to you, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 05382, and I would tender this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6253, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, this is a document that reproduces the text of an article from Tanjug on the 17th of May, 1992, and under number 1 and it indicates that Tanjug reported that a meeting was held in Sokolac on the 17th of May, 1992, with representatives of the government of the RS, the Serb autonomous region of Romanija, municipalities of Olovo and Rogatica, and representatives of the Belgrade-based association of the citizens of Romanija region, and it indicates that Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and General Mladic were in attendance. Now, such a meeting did take place on the 17th of May, 1992, in Sokolac; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that this meeting was held in Sokolac on the 17th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And it's correct that at this meeting Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and General Mladic all addressed the attendees, although it was primarily Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic who spoke; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This meeting was held at the initiative of a number of our fellow citizens who live in Serbia, Montenegro. When the crisis started, they came. They were in certain positions in Serbia, and some of them were in the business community, others worked in some institutions of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time, and they came to get some information to see how they could help their own people a bit. Primarily in terms of organising activities that were aimed at providing food and so on, and they asked for a meeting with the leadership of Republika Srpska and --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. My question was: At this meeting Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and General Mladic all addressed the attendees, but it was primarily Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic who spoke; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps in terms of the questions that were being put. Most of them who had come were saying what was -- what could be done, whether Yugoslavia could be preserved, what could be done to help, and it was probably in response to some of these questions, and certainly they were not in charge of this meeting. This meeting was organised in the municipality of Sokolac and it was attended by members of the neighbouring municipalities, heads of the municipalities, MPs, businessmen. Perhaps there were over 50 of us at that meeting. And representatives of the church and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm going to remind you about what you said in the Krajisnik case about this meeting on this point, and that's at 65 ter 24876, page 22638. You were asked by Judge Orie: "You mentioned the president of the republic. Did he address the meeting? "THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] Yes. "JUDGE ORIE: You mentioned the president of the Assembly. Did he address the meeting? "THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] Yes, they all said something. It was primarily the president of the republic and the commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic, who were primarily asked to address the audience. Then Mr. Krajisnik took the floor, he made a contribution, and some other people also asked to take the floor. However, President Karadzic and General Mladic had the main say at the meeting. They were the keynote speakers." That's what you said in Krajisnik about this meeting and that's correct; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, because most of the questions were addressed to them and then they answered those questions. So I don't see anything in dispute as far as this meeting is concerned. This is a regular meeting. This is a meeting where information was being provided to a number of important people about the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Yugoslavia, and so on and so forth, nothing special. And nothing spectacular happened there and no decisions were being made. I think it was a useful meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. This article under point 3 quotes from Dr. Karadzic stating: "We know exactly what we want. We want our state in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And if they want to take Bosnia-Herzegovina out of Yugoslavia, we want to take our state out of Bosnia-Herzegovina." And under number 4: "We must continue the transformation of the JNA triggered off by Alija Izetbegovic when he suggested to Muslims and Croats that they should not join the ranks of the JNA." Do you recall Dr. Karadzic saying words along these lines at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a newspaper article. Nobody kept any minutes over there. It is possible that President Karadzic said that we were striving for preserving Yugoslavia and that we supported the Yugoslav People's Army. It was quite certain already then that the JNA had no place in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Serb people -- rather, the Assembly of the Serb republic passed a decision to the effect that on the 12th of May, five or six days before this meeting, that the army of the Serb republic be established. Now, was it the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or was it just the Serb republic? I'm not sure. Then this meeting followed at the request of a number of business people and people who cared about the area where they came from. After this a decision was made to establish the Army of Republika Srpska and to have the JNA withdrawn. They were concerned about what would happen to the Serb people in this area, and that is what President Karadzic and General Mladic were asked about. And now if the Muslims wanted to get Bosnia-Herzegovina out of Yugoslavia by force, then certainly the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina would ask for the rest in Yugoslavia, and that is what we stated by way of a plebiscite, that we would remain in Yugoslavia. This is a position, and if it was presented, it is based on the referendum question that was responded to by the people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that they wished to remain in Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think your answer's quite clear now. Now, just one last question. There were journalists present at this meeting; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, after the meeting somebody made a statement. It was Mr. Krajisnik, but journalists did not attend the meeting itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So just if I could remind you of what you said in the Krajisnik case and we can get this clear. This is at page 22637 of the transcript. You were talking about Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic, and you said: "When they started to leave, they may have been stopped by a journalist." And then you were asked: "That's what I wanted to ask you about, the contact with a journalist, one or more journalists. Did you listen to Mr. Krajisnik or Dr. Karadzic's conversations with those journalists?" And you said: "No." That's -- is that a correct understanding of the role of journalists at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, when they came out of the meeting. That's what I said a moment ago. They were not in the meeting hall. They were in front of the meeting hall. Once the meeting was over, it was logical that someone, and in particular Krajisnik, Mladic, and Karadzic, provided a statement to the journalists because that's what they were waiting for. That's what I said. They provided statements after the meeting was over. I can't say exactly who spoke to the journalists because it's only now that you've reminded me. I seem to have forgotten it. But you did jog my memory somewhat. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6254, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bjelica, at paragraph 54 of your statement you spoke about detention facilities in Sokolac and you said that Muslims suspected of taking part in sabotage and terrorist operations were detained in the elementary school in Sokolac, Cavarine and Knezina, and also at paragraph 54 you said in relation to these facilities: "I assume that the detained persons did not have the required hygiene and other facilities in such premises since they were not envisaged for such purpose." Now, at paragraph 65 of your statement, this is information that you provided over the weekend, you were asked about adjudicated facts relating to the Cavarine detention facility, and you said: "As far as I know, hygiene was satisfactory." Now, you're saying two contradictory things about Cavarine in your statement, first that hygienic facilities were inadequate and second that hygiene was satisfactory. Those are contradictory statements about this facility; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know from my contacts with the members of the VRS, units of the VRS did have temporary prisons where they temporarily held POWs or other people who were believed to have engaged in sabotage and terrorist activities and espionage. In such detention units, there were also people of Serb ethnicity who had committed a breach of discipline or an offence, things such as not responding to call-up, theft, or something of the sort. In such detention units Serbs and Muslims were held together.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I didn't ask you to give me --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Croats --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- all the information you have about these facilities. It was a very specific question. You are saying contradictory things about the Cavarine detention facility. On the one hand you said, "I assume --" you said, "I assume that the detained persons did not have the required hygienic and other facilities," and on the other hand, you're saying, "As far as I know hygiene was satisfactory." Those two statements are contradictory, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, please. It is true that hygiene measures were not satisfactory and later on toilets were introduced. It was up to ABiH [as interpreted] units to install showers and bathrooms. There were many Serbs who were detained as well. This goes for the school as well, because it was not supposed to have been used as a detention unit. It was an abandoned facility that was used by the security organs of the 2nd Romanija Brigade. Well, no one had fell ill there or had jaundice or anything. They all shared the same food as the army. The soldiers received the same food the detainees did. There was a kitchen in Knezina and the food was there -- taken from there to the front lines and to the detention units. Everyone received the same food. It is true that such things did not exist at the beginning, but as the number of detainees increased then showers were installed in order to improve hygiene. So no one complained of everything, nor did people have skin conditions there, skin diseases. Later on they were all exchanged and were safe and sound.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An intervention for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 25, page 37, these are not units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They're not to be confused with the ABHO unit which is a service. They offer protection of -- in terms of nuclear and biological and chemical threats. In any case, it's not the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nuclear, biological, chemical protection. That's the name of such units. They were present there, and they --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, you didn't visit any of these detention facilities and see the conditions first-hand, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I did not. I said that I had contacts with the VRS members and that's where my information came from. That's what I said. I never entered any such premises. It was under the control of security organs and no one had any business being there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 19836, please. Now, this is a statement given by a woman named Sema Mujanovic, born on the 5th of May, 1930, in Knezina, a housewife, so in 1992, when the events that she talks about occurred, she was a 62-year-old housewife then living in Sahbegovici. And at page one on both languages in the second paragraph, she explains how on the 28th of July, 1992, Chetniks entered her village of Sahbegovici and captured six men and six women including herself, and they were taken to the Sokolac primary school. And if we go to the next page in the English and near the bottom of the page in B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, they only took her. I see this statement for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, in any event, in this paragraph on the next page in the English and at the bottom of the B/C/S, she identified 18 other prisoners detained with her in the Sokolac primary school. And on the next page in the English and also the next page in the B/C/S, around the middle of the page in both texts, she says: "After exactly 65 days in prison, the Chetniks moved all the prisoners in the school to the village of Cavarine." And this would have been in early October based on the dates in her statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to 65 ter 06947.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness receive a question about this document so as not to amass documents that the purported question refers to?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, the next document is related.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is a letter from the Sokolac exchange commission to the president of the VRS exchange commission Dragan Bulajic, and it states that the following POWs detained in the Sokolac prison are put at your disposal. And you can see that number 8 on the list is Sema Mujanovic, and there are 17 other prisoners including a number whom she had identified as being detained with her. Now, at paragraph 54 of your statement, you said that as far as you know, Muslims who were suspected of taking part in sabotage and terrorist operations were detained in these facilities, and you made a similar claim at paragraph 65. Did you know that a 62-year-old housewife from Sahbegovici was imprisoned first in Sokolac elementary school and then in Cavarine?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I see this for the first time. I don't know what the reason for her detention was since there were women who participated in the war, taking part in operations, carrying weapons, and setting up explosives. I do not exclude the possibility that she was one of them. No one says here why she was detained, and she doesn't mention that in her statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Bjelica, you don't have a clue as to why any of the people on this list here were detained. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't interested. It was up to the security organ, and I had no right to meddle in her activities and why they were detained. They must have taken part in certain activities. There were other inhabitants who were certainly not detained. There must have been a reason why they were brought in, a justified reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, you have said that you saw in relation to both these documents I showed you, you said that this is the first time you've seen these documents. That's not actually true. You were shown both of these documents in the Krajisnik case, and in relation to this document in front of you now --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I'm saying here in this courtroom that I see it for the first time, but back then it didn't mean anything. Why would I have remembered it? It was the work of security organs. People were interviewed and then put on the list of the exchange commission. Mr. Bulajic was in Lukavica, and he was -- he put them on the list for exchange.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the witness kindly repeat the end of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, I hadn't actually asked you a question yet. The question I wanted to ask you was that, as I said, you were shown these two documents in the Krajisnik case, and when you had this document on the screen in front of you, you were asked and this is at page 22721 of the transcript: "But the reason I present that to you is to ask you this question and put it to you that in fact the Muslims detained in these facilities we've described, they were not POWs, but they were civilians, and Ms. Sema Mujanovic is an example of that; correct?" And your answer was: "Believe me, I don't know. I can't confirm this. I never heard of any of these people or most of them. I don't know whether they had been armed. I don't know what is at stake. I really can't be a judge of that. I haven't a clue." That's what you said in the Krajisnik case and that's the truth; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, what did I say a moment ago other than that? I don't know why they were brought in. There must have been a reason for their bringing in. For example, number 8, Sema Mujanovic. Perhaps someone knew she had done something. It was the assessment of the security organ that she was of interest because she had taken part in certain activities. That is why she was interviewed, and then she was offered for an exchange after a while. That's all I said. I said in my introduction that I knew from my contacts with VRS members that those were the premises used for detention used by the security organ of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this document, and I'd also like to tender the transcript page I just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are not tendering the statement itself?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will receive them both.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 06947 will be Exhibit P6255 and the transcript will be Exhibit P6256.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, at paragraph 57 of your statement, you talked about the massacre of Muslim civilians in Novoseoci in September of 1992, and you spoke about an incident several years later where you met an acquaintance whose son had committed suicide, and he said to you, "I cannot get over my son's death. This was a great tragedy. See what Krstic did to us? He took our children to Novoseoci." Now, you understood from this conversation that it was Radislav Krstic who had issued the order to kill these civilians; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Based on that conversation. That was my understanding at the time, that he took the guys there. I was so told by the father of one of them who had killed himself. I didn't even know his son was there. As I said in the statement, that was all I knew. The father of that young boy told me that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And at paragraph 57 of your statement, you said that you are certain that no one from the Sokolac Municipal Assembly knew about the incident because it had been kept secret from the public. Now, that's totally false, Mr. Bjelica. A Defence witness who just testified, Mr. Obradovic, said that he heard about the Novoseoci killings the same day they happened, and the reason he heard about them was because this was something that people were generally talking about by the evening of the day of this incident, and that's transcript page 36095 and 36096. Mr. Tupajic similarly testified that he first learned about the Novoseoci killings on the evening of the day they took place from a soldier who had passed by the crime scene and seen the bodies, and he then learned through the grapevine, as he put it, that the night before members of the 2nd Romanija Brigade had killed all the men at Novoseoci at a landfill approximately 5 kilometres from the village. And that's P5238, transcript pages 15428 to 15430. Mr. Bjelica, these killings were the talk of the town by the evening of the day they took place, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not in Sokolac at the time. What I mention in this statement is something I learned from Mr. Tupajic who expressed his doubt before me that the people in Novoseoci suffered an inglorious fate. We never had precise data as to what had happened, because no one ever forwarded it. I stand by what I said in 2006 in the Krajisnik case, and I still stand by it. There was a terrible crime in Novoseoci, but there was another crime in Novoseoci in 1942 when a unit called the Black Hand from the adjoining municipalities of Rogatica and Pale, aided by the Ustasha from Novoseoci, surrounded the church in the village, killing 57 civilians, 23 of whom were between 10 and 20 years of age, and 16 people who were younger than 10. The same day they committed a massacre in the neighbouring village of Kula where also beastly they killed 45 civilians of whom 23 were younger than 20 years of age. In total on that day in two villages 103 people were butchered and torched in the two villages of whom 60 per cent were younger than 20. This crime, as many others, where the Ustasha during the Second World War in the territory of Sokolac municipality killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's not responsive to the question. We'll have a break for 15 minutes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, at paragraph 37 of your statement, and I noticed in -- or we noticed when in the last answer you gave you appeared to be reading from a text that was not your statement. If you need to refer to something other than your statement, if you could please just indicate what the text is and your need to refer to it. At paragraph 37 you said that some Muslims in Sokolac remained in their homes nearly until the end of the war, and you cite Vrbarije as an example. Just to put that in context, sorry, it's true that by late 1992 there were very few Muslims left in the entire municipality, no more than 30 to 40 households total; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many. In any case, a majority of the Muslims left before the end of 1992. I don't know how many household exactly stayed behind. A majority left. I said that yesterday. They left in the direction of Olovo and Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. In -- I'd like to go to 65 ter 19814, please. I'm sorry, that's clearly the wrong 65 ter number, so I will come back to that. You were asked about the number of Muslims left at the end of 1992 in the Krajisnik case, and that's at page 22639 of the transcript, and you had brought a bundle of documents that were given the exhibit number D166, and which indicated prosecutions and investigations in late 1992, and you were -- when you were asked about this, you said -- about these documents, you said the police did their job within the boundaries of their capabilities under such circumstances. This is just to support the thesis that there was no anarchy, unlike some people said that everybody did what they wanted to do. Those who were involved in crimes were brought in regardless of their ethnic background. And then on the next page of the transcript the Judge asked you a question. He said: "Mr. Bjelica, one question to clarify. You said irrespective of their ethnicity, those who were involved in crimes were brought in. At that time, how many Muslims were left in the municipality?" And you said: "I don't know. In the town of Sokolac there were not many Muslims even before the war. The municipality had some 15.000 inhabitants, and 4.000 of them were Muslims. In the town itself there may have been a few dozens of households, Muslim households, and some of them exchanged property with the Serbs from other areas, so there were not that many Muslims in the town itself."
