And the Judge said: "Yes, you said 4.000 in the municipality. How many of them were left or how many families approximately?" And you said: "In 1992, towards the end of 1992, or in the second half of 1992, I can't remember exactly, very few of them left in 1990 through the villages Vrbarije or maybe some other villages that were there, and they stayed there until 1993 or 1994. The others had left after the agreement in Knezevo [sic] now with the president of the municipality of Olovo, Mr. Dzevad Abazovic, and the negotiations were led by Milan Tupajic." And then the Judge asked and this is at page 22641: "Yes. So I do understand that there were a few dozens of households in the town, whereas you have no information on the remainder of the municipality and how many still were there." And you said: "Very few, very few, maybe 30 or 40 families altogether at the most. Very few." Now, it's correct, isn't it, Mr. Bjelica, in the Krajisnik case you testified that by late 1992 there were no more than 30 or 40 Muslim households in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there is a mistake. Not Knezevo but Knezina. I see it in the English translation. In 1992 after the agreement with Mr. Dzevad Abazovic, municipal president in Olovo, and the representative of the Serbs from Olovo, Mr. Milovan Zugic, as regards the 30 or 40 families in Sokolac, perhaps there were some 12 family homes there and some 30 or 40 apartments where Muslims resided and they did not own them but had tenants -- tenancy rights. So 12 family homes in Sokolac and some of them as I said also remained in Novoseoci. Until 1993 or 1994 there were some in Burati and Vrbarije. Some even remained after the Dayton Accords, and even the remaining few left following the Dayton Accords to the area that became the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So for the most part I agree with that statement. It is correct. There's nothing to add, only perhaps to clarify a thing or two.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, just to be clear in your answer you said some of them, as I said, also remained in Novoseoci. But with respect to Novoseoci, nobody stayed; right? On the 22nd of September when the 2nd Romanija Brigade killed all the men, women and children were taken to Sarajevo. There were no Muslims left in Novoseoci at that point; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I said that it was in the second half of 1992 when they stayed, and what you say is true. After the incident in Novoseoci, no Bosniaks were left there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, in relation to Vrbarije and the neighbouring village of Burati in Rogatica, you said in your statement that these villages asked for mutual departure in late 1994, and yesterday at page 36401 you said that this was arranged with international organisations and you mentioned the ICRC. In fact, it was the RS exchange commission which arranged this departure, and on the 29th of October, 1994, the Vrbarije villagers were taken to Kula prison under police escort by the Sokolac SJB; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I don't know where they were taken to. I only know -- well, I didn't hear that they suffered any ill fate. I did hear, though, that sometime after the Dayton Accords, perhaps in 1997 or 1998, they returned to their homes and rebuilt them. I didn't hear that they suffered any harm. Some left before the Dayton Accords, some after, whereas some never even left. It is on the border between Sokolac and Rogatica. Perhaps some 15 kilometres from the seat of Sokolac municipality and some 15 kilometres away from the seat of Sokolac municipality -- of Rogatica municipality. Those villages are next to each other, and there are even houses where the building itself was is in one municipality and the land owned by the family is in the other. But in any case, they are closer to Sokolac than to Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit D3189 please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now Vrbarije, Mr. Bjelica, according to the 1991 census it had a total of 53 inhabitants and they were all Muslims. Now is that consistent with your information? This was a tiny village, 53 people, all Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. Some of them left but some of their relatives had arrived from Rogatica or perhaps Sokolac and some other villages, and they were accommodated with their relatives. There were a lot more of them then would have been correct pursuant to any census, because they felt safe there. I'm not denying the facts of the census, but after the Dayton, over 50 left, which means that there were a lot more of them accommodated there during the war. They had arrived from various villages in order to be together, just like Serbs arrived from Sarajevo Sesekovac [phoen]. Some 10.000 of them arrived in Sokolac from Sarajevo and Olovo, at least 10.000 refugees and displaced persons ended up in Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You said at paragraph 37 that these villages, referring to Vrbarije and Burati, asked to leave in order to reunite families. Now, this implies that every family in these two villages or at least the majority of them all happened to have family members living elsewhere and all of them at the exact same time decided to leave their village and their homes and their property and their livelihoods in order to move -- reunite with family members elsewhere. Mr. Bjelica, that explanation doesn't make sense. Every family is different. Every family has different circumstances. It's not possible that the collective departure of two entire villages could be attributed to family reunification; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. There were very few military conscripts in those villages. Those who were fit for military service had left before. I suppose that they were assigned to the units of BH Army or perhaps outside of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In other words, very few military conscripts lived in those villages. I don't know exactly. I'm talking about two villages, Vrbarije and Burati. I don't know how many there were, but I know that there were a lot more people living there at the time than live there according to the 1991 census. I am not denying what you've just said. I'm not contesting that. But I believe that people had arrived from Sjenica and the other villages around Kula, and they came to Sokolac and other villages, and there were a lot more living in those villages during the war than before the war. I'm not contesting your numbers or what you're saying. What matters to me the most is the fact that none of those people came into any harm's way and they returned. And nothing bad ever happened to them. That's important. And another important thing is that they returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, you didn't answer my question. I'll try it one more time. Your explanation as to why these two villages asked to leave, family reunification, doesn't make sense because every family is different and every family has different circumstances, and it's not possible that every single family at exactly the same time made the decision to reunite with family members elsewhere. That explanation doesn't hold any water; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they said we'll go with our own, with our families, with our relatives. And the same was true of the Serbs. After the Dayton Accords were signed they did not trust the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They left Sarajevo and ended up in some underdeveloped municipalities having left behind all of their property that they had amassed for a long time. It was a natural thing to do. It was only after the Dayton Accords were signed that the real transfer of the population started.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not recorded that everybody went to those area was in a majority, and especially after the Dayton. That's what the witness said. After the Dayton Accords, people went to the areas where their own people were a majority.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, the Chamber has received evidence that the security situation in Vrbarije village was very bad. The men were being taken out by the army for forced labour on the front lines, thieves were stealing cattle and searching their houses, and they had started to spend the night in the woods, and that was why they asked to leave. That's P6235. Did you know about the security situation in Vrbarije?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you are saying. I did not know that before. The first time I've ever heard it is now from you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And Mr. Tomislav Batinic, the president of Rogatica municipality testified for the Defence, and he discussed the village of Burati in Rogatica which is a village you connect with Vrbarije, and he acknowledged that at the time the people of Burati left they lived in daily fear. Did you know about that? Sorry, that's transcript page 33691 to 33695.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. In your testimony yesterday, you stated that the departure of Muslims from Knezina and Kaljina was temporary and that they returned to Sokolac "immediately after the Dayton Peace Accords." And that's transcript page 36402. And the Chamber has received demographic statistical evidence indicating that in 1997, virtually no Muslims had returned to Sokolac, and that's P4994, Annex A1, table 1N. So when you said immediately that's not true because in 1997 virtually -- or very, very few Muslims had returned to Sokolac right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that villages are now full. All the houses and religious edifices have been rebuilt. There are a lot of Muslims. They voted in the elections. They supported me in my candidacy for the president of the municipality. They voted for me. I enjoyed their support. A significant number returned. They're opening their companies. They have their households. They have their cattle. Those who have cattle sell their milk. It is true that as quite a high number of young people work in Sarajevo and Olovo, but they visit every weekend. A lot of Bosniaks have returned to Sokolac. When it comes to the very nucleus of Sokolac, it is true that people did not return there. Those houses and apartments were exchanged even before the war conflicts broke out. A majority of the Bosniaks who lived in Sokolac had an alternative. If they had an apartment in Sokolac, they had a house in Sarajevo at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's true, is it not, that after the war you had at least on one occasion publicly advocated ethnic separation and stated that you do not want to live with Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not right. It's not true that I said that we didn't want to live with Muslims. It would be best for us to live next to each other and that was at the moment the best solution. However, as some time goes by, nobody advocated a division of any kind or anything else, but just to live next to each other. And the Muslims themselves wanted that and they say the same, that this is the best and this is the best solution for the Serbs, the Muslims, and the Croats. The Dayton Accords which have been accepted by the three sides, not fully, however it put a stop to the war and today we are living together. We have the central bodies of Bosnia-Herzegovina which are functioning, so I don't know whether I have been clear enough. If you want to ask me anything else, if you need any clarifications, please go ahead, ask me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well let's look at 65 ter 24876 in this context.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is not a reference to the previous assertion, can we get the reference for the question put on line 1, page 53?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's where we're going now. Sorry, I must have misspoken. I wanted 65 ter 19837. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also we need a reference for Batinic. It's not the page that has just been quoted. This is not where we find the words that have been referred to in the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I can double-check my reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bjelica, this is a Washington Post article dated the 26th of July, 2004, and it involves an interview with you, and if we could go to page 3 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S. Now, the third paragraph in the B/C/S and the English, in fact. There's a quote from you, and it says: "We want to have a complete break from the Muslims. We did not want to live with them and we don't want to be buried near them." And then it says: "In his view," referring to you, "Bosnia has no future as a single state and the three ethnic groups should go their own way." Now, that's what you stated to this Washington Post journalist in 2004; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It is possible that I said that, but I don't know. I don't remember this text at all. What they say here, we wanted to separate completely from the Muslims. Please, the position of the Serbs is clear: Either Yugoslavia or a separate state unit for the Serbian people, if they didn't want to live in Yugoslavia. Over the night they actually took away from us the state that we had lived in before and all of that had associated of the events that happened to the Serbs in 1914 and 1941. We were afraid that we would be exterminated, that another 1 million of us would be missing, and the best for us would be to live next to each other and to co-operate pursuant to the Dayton Accords and its provisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, you said you don't know and you don't remember this text at all, but when this -- when this -- please wait for the question. When this article was put to you in the Krajisnik case, and that's at page 22737 of the Krajisnik testimony, the question was asked, the quote was given: "We wanted to have a complete break from the Muslims. We do not want to live with them and we don't want to be buried near them." Your response was: "This is taken out of context. This is not an integral conversation. This was recorded by a camera. I remember this clearly. There was a woman whose husband and two sons had been killed, and it was in that context that I said that everything that happened they did not want to live next to each other, and that is why the dead were transferred from Sarajevo." And then on the next page you said: "So this is an emotional -- this was an emotional conversation that took place at the military cemetery. You have to bear in mind context." That's what you said in the Krajisnik case about this article; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably -- or, no, certainly. Now you have jogged my memory and thank you for that. That was Jela Djuricic. Two of her sons and her husband were killed in Sarajevo in Hadzici. She lived near Hadzici. She had her house there. She left all of her property, but she exhumed her two sons and her husband. She brought the remains to Sokolac and buried them there. That was the footage and in that conversation it was said that she didn't want to leave the remains of her two sons and her husbands there. She didn't want them to be trampled over. They did not want to be buried next to them. That's Jela Djuricic. She buried two of her sons and her husband after they were killed on the threshold of their own family house in Sarajevo. And that's correct. She left everything behind. However, she did transport the remains of her dead husband and sons to Sokolac and buried them there, and she was not the only one to do that. There were hundreds of people like that. And thank you for jogging my memory. Thank you for reminding me of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And if we look at the last paragraph of this article, right at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S it says: "But Bjelica makes no effort to hide his admiration for Karadzic: "'I knew him during the war and I followed him. I would not like anything bad to happen to Radovan.'" You also said that to the journalist on this occasion; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, and I stand by that even today.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bjelica. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you are not tendering that article?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Pardon me. Yes, I am. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6257, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, your Excellency. Can we receive the precise reference for what Batinic said, the way it was interpreted in the question. And I insist on that. Re-examination by Karadzic:

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelica, while we have the document on the screen, could you please tell us whether Bosnia-Herzegovina is a unitary state today?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina is not a unitary state today. The Bosniaks are trying to unify Bosnia and Herzegovina because -- let me not elaborate here, because Bosnia-Herzegovina consists of two different entities and the Brcko district. It is true that they're trying to centralise certain positions and posts which were not defined in the Dayton Accords, but that was what the High Commissioner did by issuing unauthorised decisions after the Dayton Accords, but that was nothing short of violence that happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. In this document it is stated that as Ashdown dismissed you from your position. He accused you of having been the ring leader of a network of legal and illegal businesses that helped to protect Karadzic. Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether Ashdown or anybody else for that matter had any objections to what you did during the war? If he did have objections, what kind of objections did he have and how did you fare in all that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not have any objections to what I did during the war or to my war past, if we can call it that. The authorities had to be shaken up in Bosnia-Herzegovina, i.e., in Republika Srpska, and that's why some of the local opposition at the time tried to launch some rumours and misinformation to the officials of the high commission, and they tried to portray some people as being involved in illegal deals in order to remove them to -- from the political scene in order to push their own political agenda. Mr. Ashdown did not have a single argument for my dismissal from my position, and it later turned out that that was the fact. There were investigations by NATO and the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina and local courts, and I had never been held responsible even for a breach of discipline. No criminal reports were ever filed against me. Finally, the High Commissioner, Mr. Valentinisko [phoen] withdrew the previous decisions on my removal from position.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Since Dr. Karadzic was mentioned the Batinic transcript reference several times, I believe the reference I gave was correct: 33693 through to 33695.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In that part Batinic said that the authorities did everything to protect them and that they could only fear some idiot not the authorities themselves.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness was never shown that part but it's neither here nor there. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what kind of procedure did you have to undergo? How much time did you waste from the moment Ashdown suspended us until the moment when Mr. Valentinisko, is not recorded, rehabilitated you? How much time elapsed between the two?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A hundred months, eight years and four months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, please remember to put a pause before you start answering the question. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kind of procedure did you have to undergo? Were you remanded in custody? Were you interrogated? What was happening to you? Can you tell the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It's very difficult for me to look back. I was removed on the 7th of March 2003. I was not allowed to work in any of the state institutions. I didn't have the right to work. I did not have the right to health care or social security. I couldn't travel. My family and my friends after my removal were in a difficult position. In 2004 on the 14th of May of that year SFOR kidnapped me in Sokolac and took me in an unknown direction or at least what was an unknown direction to me. I found myself in an unknown location for 60 days from the 14th of May 2004 until the 14th of June 2004, and then from the 30th of August until the 29th September 2004. I don't want to go into details of what was going on. There were daily interrogations. I could not orientate myself either in time or in space. I didn't know where I was. I did not have access to any press. I had nothing to read. Nobody visited me. I did not have any right to legal aid. I did not have any contacts with anybody. On two or three occasions I was allowed to use a telephone and to call home just to tell them that I'm alive and well. After I was released from that detention unit, I was told that their part of the job is over, that they had no arguments to remand me in custody or to transfer me to the prosecution. They handed me over to the security organs of the Republika Srpska, and they told me they had anything to do with Mr. Bjelica. It's up to you to carry out investigation, to prosecute him. As far as we're concerned we're done with him. On the 30th of November, 2005, I voluntarily surrendered to the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina when two people were arrested. There was some unfounded accusations against me. I spent 11 months in detention and then the court rendered a not guilty verdict. The panel was presided by Meddzida Kreso, the president of the appeals chamber. So in all of these proceedings I was found not guilty and then a decision ensued on my rehabilitation. And then I filed a case with the European Court for human rights in Strasbourg. I did not receive an answer. A number of people who were removed from their positions in Bosnia-Herzegovina also filed applications with the court in Strasbourg. They were turned down by that court but my court -- my case was accepted because I brought charges against the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina for not protecting me according to the Geneva Conventions and other European legal documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. This is the price you had to pay for co-operating with me; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether you could sleep while you were in SFOR custody? Were you able to sleep? How were you treated?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was music blasting for 24 hours, 7/24 in the container where I was. There was a neon light on 24/7. I could not communicate with anybody. I was interrogated. The only thing that I had was a church calendar and -- after the three meals that were brought to the cell where I was, and I was tied in that cell most of the time. I would scratch the dates with a nail, and I remember well that it was on the 21st of May, 2004, when I was taken out for interrogation, and what I was told at the time was if you need an interpreter, you raise a thumb. If you want to go to the toilet, you raise another finger. If you want to do a number two you raise two fingers, and another signal if you needed a doctor. They took me away. They asked me about Karadzic. They asked me if I knew anything about his whereabouts, the whereabouts of Mr. Karadzic at the time. I also had to take a lie detector test. I had to undergo all that. And one day I was taken out and then they told me you are being taken to Guantanamo. I was put in a car or a helicopter, I don't know. I was driven here and there. And then they returned me and they told me you're not going to Guantanamo but to The Hague, and then not to The Hague but to the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then they took me out of the vehicle in which I was being transported. They moved me a bit further. I always had headphones on my ears. I had to have dark glasses and a hat on my head, a balaclava. I was handcuffs, they pushed me, and I felt something hard behind my back like an obstacle, and then in front of me I saw five or six armed soldiers with long barrelled rifles. And then after that -- let me not go into any more details. Then they returned me back to the room. It was already summer, the days were warm, and there was a ventilator by the door which brought in hot air. I also sensed some unnatural smells. I realized that those were some irritants. I don't know what they were. But in any case, what I had to go through I would not wish upon the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on to a different topic now. The authorities in Sokolac, did they expel Muslims? Did they leave because they were expelled by the authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's what I have already said, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 19836, the statement of Sema Mujanovic, just for the sake of seeing one sentence. 19836.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm going to read out the sentence. It's the second one. "Out of fear because of the Chetniks, most of the inhabitants of the village moved in the direction of Olovo." How does this tally with what you know?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's for sure. I've already said on the basis of the agreement initiated by Mr. Abazovic and Mr. Milovan Zugic with the leadership of the municipality of Sokolac, the population, the Bosniak population was supposed to be moved temporarily to the municipality of Olovo, and the Serb municipality temporarily to the municipality of Sokolac until the situation calmed down. So this is certainly incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Obradovic, is he an assemblyman in the Municipal Assembly? Actually, tell us that first.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm asking that because on page 43 in line 18 it was put to you that you had said that no one in the Municipal Assembly and the municipal parliament knew about this. However, you were confronted with the following: that Mr. Obradovic heard about that before you. Tell us, what was Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic was then in the public security station. I don't know whether he was chief or commandeer of the police, but he was not a member of the SDS then and he could not have been an assemblyman in the Municipal Assembly of Sokolac, and I know for sure that he was not a member of the SDP or the reformist forces or the movement for Yugoslavia or the SDA or the MBO. These were the parties that participated in the government of the municipality of Sokolac. Mr. Obradovic was a person who did not belong to any political party. He had a job with the police, but then maybe he joined a political party after he retired. Maybe he signed something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. When you answered the questions that had to do with the perpetrators of the killing in Novoseoci, and also you deal with that in Article 57 of your statement, in this -- the father of this man said see what Krstic did to us. Did he say that Krstic was personally in charge of this action, or did he mean that as commander he was responsible for his son?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly whether he was in charge, but it is certain that nothing could be done in the brigade without the brigade commander. That is to say that decisions were executive for lower-ranking officers and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 57 you say: "At the time I was not there." You didn't know that this young man was there. And for yourself you say: "I did not know under whose command this incident occurred." Can you tell us whether you found out who commanded this lower-ranking unit?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think that question was a little misleading because the full sentence in the statement was: "I had not known up to that moment," mean the conversation with the acquaintance, "that this young man had been there, nor did I know under whose command the incident had been committed." So the way the sentence is phrased he then discovered that occasion and the question was I think misleading in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm just quoting this but it's not for the purpose of citing it, I'm just asking him whether he knew which lower ranking unit this was. It certainly wasn't the whole brigade.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was not the whole brigade, but I don't know which lower-ranking unit it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 19 it was suggested that you and I sent units to Croatia. Could you tell the Trial Chamber who General Uzelac was and where his headquarters was in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Uzelac, I think, was the commander of the Krajina Corps, as far as I can remember, with headquarters in Banja Luka. He was the commander of the Banja Luka Corps or the Knin corps, some corps up there. He wasn't in Sarajevo. And we could not send units to the front line. Rather, we encouraged military conscripts to respond to the JNA call-up in order to preserve Yugoslavia and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you take a look at this. On page 14 you were asked about the war hospital. Did any official ask for that -- or, rather, was this within the system, or was this the SAO Romanija that was doing this on its own apart from the system as such?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military hospital, rather, the hospital of the Main Staff in Sokolac was established by the JNA. It was in the days of the JNA that a number of doctors were relocated or sent to a particular facility in Sokolac that was built by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was called Zavod za Medicinu, 7.500 square metres. The command of the Sarajevo district decided to establish a temporary hospital there. They sent a number of doctors from the Sarajevo military hospital there. As far as I know -- well, no, I know for sure that Mr. Nakas was there from the military hospital. He was a Bosniak. He was the first doctor that came to that hospital and worked there, and he worked there, and then also a number of Croats and Slovenes worked in this military hospital throughout the war, and even some Bosniaks. And this military hospital catered to all who needed their assistance irrespective of ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P6252. Could we have a look at that, please. May I remind the other participants that the brother of the late Abdulah Nakas who testified here confirmed that his brother went out to Pale and Sokolac when the war started. P6252. Could we have document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Please read the first paragraph only. Could you read it out, just the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. "In connection to the agreement of the Chief of General Staff of the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the chief of the Medical Corps administration, the command of the 2nd Military Distinct, we hereby submit the list of necessary medical and sanitary equipment for the wartime hospitals of Podromanija-Sokolac. The newly erected building with about 7.000 square metres of useful space will be used as a wartime hospital and should be provided with technical and technological equipment ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. We don't need to read any further. What's the role of the SAO Romanija here?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SAO Romanija did not play any role here because this was passed by the command of the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo, and one of the persons who was the most deserving in terms of setting up this hospital was Mr. Nakas, Mr. Lazarevic, Tausan, and the others who came and who established this hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were military personnel. They were lieutenant-colonels and colonels of the JNA, and it was on orders from their Supreme Command that they went up there and established that institution.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about the organs of the SAO. First of all, can you tell us whether the SAO Romanija -- actually, I'm not asking you whether it was proclaimed or whatever, but was it part of the government as such? Did it have executive organs and did it pass executive decisions?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. In 05360 in paragraph 4, it says they reached a conclusion, or rather elements of the SAO should strike a balance in terms of their policies. Could you tell the Trial Chamber what the difference is between a conclusion and a decision?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A conclusion is recommended, whereas a decision is implemented. To view the situation in the neighbouring municipalities and to behave in a similar way. I mean, that would be it. As for decisions, a decision has to be carried out, whereas a conclusion is not binding. However, a decision is binding.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Treanor, an expert witness of the Prosecution, in his report, P2536 in paragraph 137, he said: "However, it seems that the SAO Romanija-Birac never existed and that SAO Romanija and Birac continued to exist during the summer of 1992."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: We do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Further on in paragraph 38 he says: Like in the previous stage, the community of municipalities under Serb control information about the structure and functioning of the SAO primarily stem from the ARK. As far as other SAOs are concerned, only a small number of documents are accessible in terms of organs that belonged to them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Again, we do not have the document so this is not a quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters are not following.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: What was read out was interpreted but we don't have the original document so it cannot be considered as a quotation as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Also, Your Honours, this is an expert report which cites in detail quotes. This witness is not an expert on the SAOs. I don't know what exactly Dr. Karadzic wants to ask, but first of all it appears to be leading and secondly it could be misleading because, of course, the witness doesn't have all of the sources and material that Dr. Treanor relied upon, so this isn't an appropriate exercise in my submission.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In paragraph 138, the Prosecution expert witness complained that the other SAOs except for the ARK Krajina did not have any documents. Can you tell us how many documents remained after the SAO Romanija?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know about this programme. Somebody must have just written this and had it published, but except for a few releases that were issued by either the prime minister or the minister of information, but anyway there weren't any other documents because this did not function. I've already said that the territory was not contiguous and the seat was in Sarajevo and we never met. The Assembly never met to decide on the further fate of the SAO Romanija.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, you mentioned on page 6 that this plan, this programme, was not before the Assembly, the one that was produced by the government. Why would it have to be before the Assembly? Who approves government documents?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, government -- the government itself passes its own documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And which organ approves these documents so that the government could go on working?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The peoples Assembly. And then the president of the republic by his own decrees confirms certain laws.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if it is convenient, shall we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly. I was just about to finish right now, Excellency. Thank you, Mr. Bjelica, for your work, thank you for your testimony, and thank you for your great work on behalf the Serb people, and I owe you a great deal because of the suffering that you've been through on account of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I didn't want to raise this in open court. I raised it with the Defence previously and expressed my concerns about these continued and now growing expressions of directed at witnesses at the conclusion of their testimony. Recently it prompted an unfortunate diatribe by a witness. In any event, I think they're clearly inappropriate, particularly since they've been expanding in scope and length, and I would ask that Mr. Karadzic be encouraged to desist from this practice. As I say, I raised it with the Defence initially and said I didn't want to do it in open court, but if it persisted I would raise it in open court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, if you could advise Mr. Karadzic what to do and what not to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I'm doing this, Excellencies, because I'm not in a position to say good-bye to the witnesses. I do not have the opportunity to say good-bye on a personal note to witnesses once they've finished testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, saying good-bye is one thing. Making extended commentary is quite another, and you must realise that is it has absolutely no evidential value whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is absolutely clear to me, but this is a matter of courtesy. And it's true, too. However, if this is not allowed, then somebody should express their gratitude to the witnesses who appear here on behalf of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, every witness has the gratitude expressed by this court for attending as you well know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's quite inappropriate in the Chamber's view to say what you said, and you had the opportunity during your proofing if necessary. In any event, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Bjelica. On behalf of the Chamber and the Tribunal, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, and I would just like to say that the persons belonging to the service that takes care of us and escorts us while we're in The Hague have done a great job and I would like to thank them once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll rise all together. We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before Mr. Cekic makes the solemn declaration yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As I discussed with Mr. Robinson during the adjournment, there was some confusion about the witness order list arising from conflicting information that was sent. I only mention that because it -- Mr. Zec's understanding was and other understandings were that this witness would be testifying tomorrow. It's not a problem. Mr. Zec is prepared to proceed so there won't be a delay. I only mention that because -- so that the Court, if necessary, may provide Mr. Zec with a little latitude in his examination as a result of the circumstances in which he finds himself, but I don't think there will be any sort of problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I just also want to express my appreciation to the Prosecution, and we apologise for any confusion that we caused them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On my part as well. I thought it was Mr. Kralj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: At one point the Prosecution had asked us to switch the witnesses and then we thought that they had -- there was no need for that any longer so we switched them back, but we didn't communicate it very well. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Mr. Cekic. Would you make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cekic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Cekic, I must draw your attention to a certain Rule of procedure and evidence that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E). Under this Rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that would amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question, but in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Cekic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cekic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cekic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I need to ask you to speak slowly as I will try to do, and we need to pause between question and answer so as to have everything recorded in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, did you provide a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have 1D7982 in e-court. Could I ask you to look at the screen before you. Do you see that statement of yours before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: I can see it, but it's too small for me to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have a hard copy of your statement with you? In that case, we would ask the Chamber to allow you to rely on it if necessary?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't. I was told to only bring my glasses and passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you read the statement and signed it?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Kindly pause before answering.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the last page so that the witness is able to see his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it your signature?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you told the Defence team, or do you have any need to make certain corrections? Is it completely accurate?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: For the most part it faithfully conveys my words, and there's nothing that I'd like to correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions today, would your answers be basically the same?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The gist would be the same.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Excellencies, I seek to tender this statement under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're also offering three associated exhibits, none of which are on the 65 ter list. We would ask that they be added as we hadn't interviewed this witness at the time the document was filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: No, President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll admit the statement as well as the three associated deliberates.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The statement is Exhibit D3236 and the three documents will be Exhibit D3237 through to Exhibit D3239.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will read out a summary of Mr. Cekic's statement in the English language. [In English] Mr. Gojko Cekic was born on 6th of July, 1936, in Podgorica village, Bosanska Gradiska municipality. Now resides in Bijeljina city. Gojko Cekic worked at the Hadzici garrison until he retired at the end of 1990 with the rank of lieutenant-colonel. In August 1992, following the formation of the VRS, he was mobilised and assigned to the Bijeljina garrison. In August 1994, he was assigned to duty as the commander of the Ekonomija collection centre in Batkovic village where he was charged with organising the centre pursuant to the order of the corps commander. This was done at all times in accordance with the provisions of the Geneva Conventions relevant to the treatment of prisoners of war. All procedures here were in keeping with the current rules and regulations of the entire army. The individuals brought to the Ekonomija collection centre were soldiers captured on lines facing the units of the 28th Division of BH Army as it is clear from the statements of individuals leaving the centre and from other lines of confrontation. Interviews were conducted with captures by members of the military police and security organs of the corps in order to ascertain information about the prisoners' unit and command and uncover any war crimes against combatants, Serbian combatants, and civilians. The relationship between the guards and the prisoners was correct and at any -- at times friendly. The prisoners ate the same food as the guards and the VRS soldiers in the barracks, were given sufficient shelter and heating in the winter, and were given regular preventative medical check-ups by mobilised doctors. Gojko Cekic never ordered nor allowed any of his subordinates to physically abuse prisoners in any way, in any violation of order issued by him -- and any violation of orders issued by him was punished. Gojko Cekic was ordered to allow unhindered access to the centre to the ICRC officials who had no complaints about the prisoners' treatment. The Ekonomija collection centre was disbanded with the order of superior command in -- in the autumn of 1995 when the truce came into effect. [Interpretation] At this point I have no questions for Mr. Cekic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Cekic. As you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is through your written witness statement in lieu of your oral testimony, and you'll now be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Cekic.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let me first clarify something that you said in your statement. In paragraph 12 you referred to document 1D06076, which has been admitted associate exhibit, and if we can have it please on the screen. You told us, Mr. Cekic, that the Batkovic centre had 4.310 blankets and 315 sleeping mattresses. For this assertion, you refer to paragraph 2 and paragraph 4 of the document from 1996 which you're going to see on the screen in a minute. And I would like to look at these two paragraphs of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I have number 1D06076. That's one of the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Cekic, if you look at the screen, I would like to paragraph 2 and 4. So -- and paragraph 4 says that in 1993, Bijeljina military post 7109 was given 3.710 blankets and 110 mattresses. First, Mr. Cekic, military post 7109 was a logistic base, was it?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So the numbers that you provide in paragraph 12 represent the totality of these items that apparently went through Batkovic throughout its existence, and this was -- this was not something that you had at your disposal; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question, but as for the figure of 3.000 -- just one moment. Four thousand three hundred and ten blankets and three hundred and fifteen mattresses, I returned that equipment in 1996 to the units they belonged to; that is to say, to the base, to the barracks of the unit where they had come from, that and the rest of the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: That's exactly what I want to ask you about, because in the document it says that this material was given to logistic base in 1993, which means it was not there in 1996. That's exactly the issue I want to raise with you.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: No. No. A moment, please. Did I sign this document at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes. You did.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: How could I have signed it in 1993 when I came there in 1994? This is a mistake with the date. In any case, they were handed over in 1996, not in 1993. Only the vehicle -- no, not even the vehicle. It was all handed over in January 1996. In 1993, I was not at the collection centre, and I couldn't have signed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I was not suggesting that you were in 1993 there, but what it says document that the material was given to the logistic base in 1993. In any event, let me ask you this: The main provider of these items was the ICRC, was it?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: Part of it did arrive from the International Red Cross. However, the rest came from the barracks such as parts of tents, mattresses, wooden frames for beds, weapons, et cetera. Please bear with me. As for the ICRC, we for the most part received some of the blankets. That's why there were so many. They were given us by the International Red Cross, quite a few blankets.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So while we're on this topic, let me show you another related document, and this time I want to focus to what you said in paragraph 11 about the prisoners having been able to take hot showers every day at Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 24877. And, Mr. President, I believe we have not received translation of this document yet, so we'll try to work with B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is another hand-over receipt issued in 1996 following the disclosure of Batkovic. It refers to the hand-over of the premises and items used at Batkovic. Item 1 refers to the offices. Item number 2 refers to the reception centre office, sorry. Item number 3, hangar and other facilities. Mr. Cekic, if you look at item number 3 and what is listed there, can you see 1 field bath and one field toilet with two cabinets?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. I see what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, there is no on the list five or six showers that you describe in your statement, is it?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: It is correct. Can I provide an explanation for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is the document that lists all the items at Batkovic at the time, including, and as we saw in the previous document, spoons, so the toilets that you talk about should be listed here but they are not there.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's not there. Do you know where the difference lies? This is the materiel we had received, not myself but those who held my position prior to 1993. They received it from the Ekonomija farm. The same goes for the bath and toilet boxes. As for the part that was additionally added, I see, for example, wire which is missing and the five or six toilet boxes and baths. They're not to be found here. I can't exactly explain why they aren't, but they were also not issued to us, the equipment needed for such baths.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If you look the signatures, among these there is your signature and the signature of Milenko Lujic. Can you confirm that Milenko Lujic is Surgeon First Class Lujic that you referred to in paragraph 15 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can you explain what these letters VIK that we see before his name stand for?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: He was the company clerk as we referred to them. As for the VIP, I don't really know what it stands for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And he --

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: In any case, he was the recording clerk at the collection centre. He was in charge of issuing and receiving equipment and I only verified the lists he kept. He was in charge of the office.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: In line 17, it should be VIK instead of VIP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And before that Lujic was in charge of the guards at the camp, was he?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: He was also the guard commander or one of. There were a few of them. Once every month for a week he commanded the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You are not aware -- aware of him being punished or disciplined for any offence, are you?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, he was not summoned, interviewed, or sanctioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This Chamber has received evidence that during 1992-1993, Milenko Lujic was involved in beatings, torture, and hiding of the prisoners from the ICRC. Do you know about this, Mr. Cekic?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: I couldn't have been aware of it, because in 1992 and 1993 I was never at the collection centre, nor did I know the people working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I refer to P48, page 8 to 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, this Chamber has received evidence that a prisoner by the name of Ferid Zecevic or professor, how he was called, was beaten to death by the guards in the presence of Veljko Stojanovic for whom you say in paragraph 22 that he was a guard commander at Batkovic. Husein Curic and 70-year-old Zulfo Hadziomerovic were also beaten to death. These and other murders and beatings, Mr. Cekic, were not result of a drunk prisoner attacking guards and then them defending themselves with the rifle as you describe it in paragraph 18, but the result of the cruel conditions imposed on the Batkovic prisoners. Were you aware of this, Mr. Cekic?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: No. I wasn't aware of the conditions or of the fact that people were being beaten or that anything else that was not permitted was done. At the time I was not at the collection centre in Batkovic. I couldn't have been aware of it and I didn't hear it being discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Before that P48 you referred to. It may be something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now I was referring to P59, page 873, and P3212, page 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, this Chamber has received evidence that there were up to 3.000 prisoners at Batkovic. They slept on the concrete floors. The toilet was a deep hole in the ground. There was no medical treatment. A young man from Brezevo Polje died from diabetes. Some prisoners had heart attacks. So were you aware, Mr. Cekic, of these conditions at the Batkovic before you were appointed commander?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of such conditions or incidents or cases or such things occurring before I was appointed commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I refer to P58, page 11; P111, page 491 to 43 -- 493, and P3212, page 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, the prisoners were forced to labour on the fields at the front lines and abandoned Muslim houses; that is, to remove these goods from these houses. Those that were forced to labour at the front lines, they were used to dig trenches, to carry ammunition, and chop firewood. Some of the prisoners got killed and some wounded while performing this labour. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that. At the time when I was there, that did not happen. Prisoners went to work --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'm asking this because you were in security organ as you say of the 3rd Mixed Artillery Regiment. So you haven't heard or so prisoner carrying ammunition? Would you like me to repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: No, I understand your question, but now the volume has been stepped up so I can hear it. No, I was in the 3rd Mixed Artillery Regiment. I went out into the field, I visited units, but in those units there were never any prisoners who carried ammunition. So that was not the case for the 3rd MAP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I refer to P58, page 11; P59, page 875 to 876; P84, page 9; P111, page 495 to 496; and P3212, page 46, 47. Can we have now on the screen 65 ter 24879, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, is 24877 being tendered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Hand-over receipt.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Yes, Mr. President. We would like to tender, but we don't have translation, so I presume --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we mark it for identification pending English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P6258, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is a decision to release 16 prisoners from Batkovic and send them to -- to the Yugoslav river shipping company, Belgrade, to conduct compulsory work service. This decision refers in its introductory part to the order of the president of the RS Presidency, the IBK order, and the request of the Yugoslav River Shipping Company. Mr. Cekic, was this company listed among the companies that you referred to in paragraph 19 of your statement when you say that the companies asked for prisoners to labour?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat what the name of that company was and where its seat was?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The seat was in Belgrade, and the company name is Yugoslav River Shipping Company.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: No, never heard of that, that prisoners went outside the territory of Republika Srpska, especially not to Belgrade. This is the first I hear of it. And I don't believe that. I mean, I'm not saying. Anything is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: One can presume that shipping company can have some premises at Sava River, Sava River near Bijeljina, but in any event, you haven't heard of this company?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we would object at this point because the witness hasn't been able to confirm anything. It looks like it has some elements of authenticity, but I was just checking myself because it refers to an order from the Presidency of 8 September 1992, and I was unable to find that order. So I have some questions about whether this should be admitted. So perhaps absent a showing of provenance it can be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear from you, Mr. Zec?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I'm given sufficient time, I can show to you that these 16 names are listed in another exhibit that you have before you, which is P03213, which verifies that these people were detained at Batkovic and these dates when they were sent to this -- to labour, so which suggests that this document is authentic document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it necessary for you to rise, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's only for the purpose of trying to ensure consistency, Mr. President, but I take it from your question that you would not wish further comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having heard Mr. Zec's submission, would you like to add anything, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6259, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Mr. Cekic, about the ICRC visits to Batkovic before the time that you were there. This Chamber has received evidence that some of the Batkovic prisoners were removed from the camp prior to the visits of the ICRC. These were mostly elderly, children, and some others. The guards stood or posed for the missing and killed prisoners. The prisoners were instructed what to say when the ICRC arrives. Were you aware, Mr. Cekic, of this practice at Batkovic with respect to the ICRC before your service there?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can just answer about what I -- about what I know. I can only say about the period when I was there, and if you want me to talk about that, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: That's in your statement, so we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I refer to P59, page 877 to 878; then P84, page 8; and P2929, page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, Major Djoko Pajic, who you referred to in paragraph 4 of your statement, who was in charge of Batkovic before you, is currently on trial before the local court in Bijeljina for crimes committed at Batkovic together with Petar Dmitrovic, Ljubisa Misic, and Djordje Krstic. Can you confirm this, Mr. Cekic?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that there was a trial like that in Bijeljina. I don't know whether it's over and I don't know what the outcome is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's talk about Batkovic at the time when you were in charge. Among these 120 prisoners that you say arrived to Batkovic after the fall of Srebrenica, among them there were wounded, elderly, and children; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: Among them there weren't any children. There weren't many elderly people either. There were people there, say, up until the age of 55. I could not really tell then how old people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Some of these wounded died at Batkovic as a result of the conditions they were subjected to; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. What is correct is that three persons died, those who were wounded in Srebrenica during the breakthrough. They were given medical assistance when they came to the collection centre in Batkovic. However, after that, after a few days, they died nevertheless. That was established by a doctor. The International Red Cross was informed, so everything was done in accordance with regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's talk about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 24880.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is a list of seven wounded people brought by the UNPROFOR from Potocari to the health centre Bratunac on 17 July 1995. The Chamber has heard evidence about the MSF field hospital in Potocari, but here on this document do you see item number 4, Hajrudin Alic? Hajrudin Alic died at Batkovic. Do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: Well, I remember that there were several persons by the name of Hajrudin. Whether that's the one, I don't know. Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I mention this evacuation of wounded from Potocari, and that's P04752, page 10 to 12; P04175, page 25 -- 24-25. Can we have now 65 ter 23185.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this being tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I will use one more document, so then I can ask to be tendered together. And this is a list -- this is not correct document. It should be 03185. And this is a list of 22 people that were transferred under guards on 18 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the number again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The last seven names on this list are the seven that were brought to Bratunac the day before that he saw on the previous list. Item number 19 is Hajrudin Alic who is the -- whose name we also saw a moment ago. These 22 people, Mr. Cekic, these were among the first few Srebrenica prisoners that you received at Batkovic after the fall of Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: Right now I cannot remember exactly the names and surnames of these people who came, but I do remember that a group of some 20 persons came.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can now tender these two lists, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P6260 and 6261 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have now P03213. And this is a list of the Batkovic prisoners. We would need e-court page 9 for the B/C/S. Mr. President, this document, the translation does not contain all the names that appear on the B/C/S version simply because it's a list of names.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Cekic, can you have a look at item number 121 on this page. It is Hajrudin Alic, son of Alija, that we talk about for some time now. He arrived at Batkovic on 18 July 1992. Next to it there's a date, 24 July 1995, and in the last column it says that he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we now have B/C/S e-court page 133.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A question, your Excellencies, not to have things piled up in these questions, and even I cannot see where these questions are going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's see. Let's hear the question. Let's wait and see. Shall we proceed, Mr. Zec?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And my basic question was about these wounded who died at Batkovic, and we are talking about them. So I want to just point to two names that appear on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And now on this page, item 213 is Ramo Mujic, son of Mustafa. He was brought to Batkovic on 25 July, 1995, and he died on 7 August 1995. Now I can -- can we have 65 ter 24883.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you have no question for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, I will have. After I show one more document I will have a witness -- because what I'm going to show next is the local witness statement of a person who saw these people at Batkovic, these two that I just mentioned. And this is a local statement or questionnaire of Bekir Ademovic. Can we have last page of this document. And this person, Mr. President, Bekir Ademovic is also listed in the list of 22 people taken from Bratunac to health centre, from Bratunac to Batkovic on 18 July 1994 -- 1995. And in B/C/S we would need -- go back to page before. And one more page, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So here Bekir Ademovic said that Hajrudin Alic had a stomach wound. Bekir did not see him receive any medical treatment until the arrival of the Red Cross. Hajrudin died at Batkovic. Bekir also said in the next paragraph that Ramo from Babuljica village, Srebrenica, could not take any food as a result of the beating that he suffered when he was captured. Ramo died at Batkovic. And these are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What page do we have it on the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Should be last page in English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And these two names I've been showing earlier in the log-book that we saw. So, Mr. Cekic, the realities that people were dying at Batkovic as a result of the conditions they were subject to, were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: No. They were not dying because of the conditions in the Batkovic centre. They died as a consequence of their wounding during the breakthrough from Srebrenica. This can be confirmed by Dr. Blagojevic, who established that they had died, and this can be confirmed. I believe that for each and every person who died in the Batkovic centre there is a report of the International Committee of the Red Cross, because they were called in every time a person died. Also, they were present when this first group of 22 persons came to Batkovic, and together with us in the afternoon they took care of them. A doctor was called in straight away. Since food had not been provided for that day we sent the driver to town. Bread and tins were purchased for them. They were in a sorry state. No one could have died as a consequence of the conditions in Batkovic because the conditions were not that bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have English page 8 and B/C/S page 2 of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: What, Mr. Cekic, this person Bekir Ademovic said that during his detention at Batkovic, he saw Vujic, he's a deputy camp commander, beat Alija from Cerska, Zaim from Tokoljak village in Srebrenica, and Alija Canic from Janja. So, Mr. Cekic, these prisoners were subjected to beatings and torture at Batkovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: That is not correct. While I was commander of the collection centre there, no one beat anybody up. No one abused anyone. Persons from the ICRC came regularly. They would meet them, and none of us were present during those meetings. After these meetings I always asked are there any objections in terms of our work and what do you think about this? Persons from the International Red Cross never said that there were any complaints concerning beatings or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Was there any Vujic deputy commander at Batkovic? Or this perhaps could be Lujic, Milenko Lujic, that we talked about earlier.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is Milenko Lujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Could we now have P03213.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is again the list of Batkovic prisoners that we looked at earlier. Mr. Cekic, I asked you whether elderly and children who were detained at Batkovic during your time there, so now we're going to have a look at some of their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have B/C/S e-court page 9. And I believe, Mr. President, we can work from this point with B/C/S only.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Item number 136 is Ramo Ahmetovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We need B/C/S e-court page 9, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So item number 136 is Ramo Ahmetovic, son of Selve, born in 1924. And, Mr. Cekic, you told us in paragraph 19 that you were the oldest at Batkovic. Here we see that the prisoner by the name of Ramo Ahmetovic was 12 years older than you, Mr. Cekic. Did you see him there?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO CEKIC
utterances.text: Well, I personally do not remember him, but he was present there. However, when I said that I was among the eldest persons there, that had to do with those prisoners of war who were there up until then, July 1995. However, in 1995, at the end of July, these prisoners who were brought in were persons -- I mean, who were brought from the breakthrough or from combat. Now, whether he had joined these soldiers of the BH Army and then together with them did he come --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you. You and answered my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we now have e-court page 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Item number 29 is Haris Dzenanovic, born in 1978, 17 at the time. Item number 31 is Mersad Dzanic, born in 1980, 15 at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have e-court page 78.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Item number 223 is Nermin Hakic, born in 1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Perhaps I should show only one additional page. Can we have e-court page 139. E-court page 131, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
